MacPaint gives you total freedom

To doodle. To cross-hatch. To spray paint. To fill-in. To erase.
“With MacPaint, for the first time, a personal computer can produce virtually any image the human hand can create. Because the mouse allows the human hand to create it.”— Apple, 1984

Forty-two years later, the same promise holds. Every tool, every pattern, every fat-bit pixel — back on your desktop, as a real Mac app.

Twenty tools.
Zero learning curve.

The original palette, pixel for pixel. If you can point, you already know how to use every one of them.

Lasso

Hugs the edges of whatever you draw, so you can lift it cleanly off the page.

Selection

Draw a marquee, then move, stretch, copy or flip what’s inside.

Grabber

Slide the whole page around beneath your window.

Text

Captions, labels and headlines, set in classic bitmap type.

Paint Bucket

Pours any of the 38 patterns into any closed shape.

Spray Can

Airbrush, the one-bit way. Spray with any pattern.

Brush & Pencil

Big expressive strokes, or one perfect pixel at a time.

Line & Eraser

Dead-straight lines. And a clean slate when you need one.

Rectangles

Hollow or filled, square corners or rounded.

Ovals & Polygons

Circles, freeform blobs and polygons — outlined or filled.

Tip Hover a tool — it highlights just like the 1984 palette.
The pattern palette

Thirty-eight patterns.
One bit each.

Texture

Bricks, scales, weaves, dithers. Eight by eight pixels, tiled to infinity. Every pattern here was lifted straight from the port’s palette. Click one.

Paint with it.
Right here.

Pick a pattern above, then drag across the canvas. It’s the paintbrush tool, in your browser, in one glorious bit.

On every Macintosh ad

“MacPaint produces virtually any image the human hand can create.” — Newsweek insert caption.

“Created from an early scan by Bill Atkinson of a 1920’s print that belonged to Steve Jobs. It appeared on the cover of the original box, diskette label, and manual for MacPaint.”

— Susan Kare, kareprints.com

Made in MacPaint.
Before it shipped.

In 1983, Susan Kare used Bill Atkinson’s work-in-progress to make the Mac team’s party invites, report covers and demo art. Here’s the proof that a mouse could draw.

Macintosh TV spot · 1984

“It can draw a picture or it can draw conclusions.”

We’ll stick to the pictures.

Under the hood

Now native on
Apple silicon.

No emulator. No ROM images. No 128K of memory to share. Just a real Mac app with a 1984 soul — instant to launch, sharp on Retina, and right at home next to everything else in your Dock.

Native
1 bit

Pure black and white. Every pixel is either on or off — exactly like 1984.

38

Patterns in the palette, extracted pixel-for-pixel from the classic set.

20

Classic tools, from the lasso to the filled polygon.

0

Emulation layers between you and the canvas.

Native

Feels like the Mac you have.

Real windows, real menus, real keyboard shortcuts. The look is 1984; the app is 2026.

Faithful

Fat bits, not fake bits.

Tool icons, menus and patterns follow the original MacPaint layout — File, Edit, Goodies, Font, FontSize, Style.

Built with Codex

One developer. One AI pair.

Designed and built by Artem Palkin together with Codex — a love letter to Bill Atkinson and Susan Kare.

Forty-three years
in the making.

MacPaint and MacWrite are the first two programs for the new Mac.

MacPaint Native Mod

Enhanced.
Original at heart.

Two new powers, hidden behind one checkbox in About MacPaint. Turn them off, and it’s pure 1984 again.

128 K

Of memory to share. Again — if you want it.

512×342

The screen MacPaint was born on. 1 bit per pixel.

576×720

One page. Every pixel within reach.

10

MCP tools that let an AI pick up the pencil.

Original mode

Macintosh 128K. Back in the box.

A virtual heap, floppy-speed saves and classic mouse acceleration — the limits MacPaint was built to beat. BYTE, February 1984: Mac Paint “manipulates the drawing on a bit-by-bit level,” and FatBits “allows us to erase or paint on a pixel-by-pixel basis.” — Gregg Williams, BYTE, Feb 1984

MCP

Now it draws with you.

Ask your AI for a house, a tree, a whole page of ideas — and watch it paint, pixel by pixel, in real MacPaint. Every stroke one Undo away. Every pixel still black and white.
